grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: mi libro; mis libros. Nuestro patio; nuestra sala; nuestros libros; nuestras sillas.
grammar.note_en:
A possessive links a noun to a person or group: mi libro means “my book”, tu libro “your book” when speaking to one familiar person, and su libro “his/her/your book” according to context. These are short possessives placed before the noun. They normally replace an article: mi madre, not la mi madre. A possessive can express a relationship as well as ownership: mi madre means “my mother”, not that a person is property. Tu has no written accent when it means “your”; tú with an accent is the subject pronoun “you”. The chapter contrasts ¿Es tu sala, Elena? (“Is it your room, Elena?”) with ¿Y tú, Ana? (“And you, Ana?”).

Mi and tu do not change for a feminine noun: mi padre and mi madre mean “my father” and “my mother”. They take -s for a plural noun: mis amigos means “my friends”; tus amigos, “your friends”. The number agrees with the things or people named after the possessive, not the number of owners. One person can have mis libros, “my books”; several people can have nuestro patio, “our courtyard”. Su follows the same short pattern: su libro, “her book”; sus libros, “his books” in the scene about Elena’s brother. Su does not identify the owner’s gender. When Elena says Es su caja after La caja es de Luis, su refers to Luis. When she says Es su libro after El libro blanco es de mi madre, it refers to her mother. The preceding words resolve that difference.

Su is also the possessive used with usted, the respectful singular “you”. Usted comparte su libro means “You share your book”, addressing Elena’s mother. The verb has the third-person ending even though the listener is being addressed. Do not assume every su means “your”; identify the speaker, listener and previously named possessor. De makes the relationship explicit: la caja de Luis is “Luis’s box”, el libro de mi madre “my mother’s book”. De does not take an English apostrophe. Del patio means “of the courtyard”, combining de and el, as before. The reading uses de with names and family roles to clear up whose objects are being discussed.

Nuestro changes for both gender and number of the noun: nuestro patio, “our courtyard”; nuestra sala, “our room”; nuestros libros, “our books”; nuestras sillas, “our chairs”. The -o/-a and -s endings describe the noun’s grammatical gender and number, not the gender of the speakers. Ana includes herself and the other users in the group. These short forms stand before nouns; this chapter does not introduce the longer independent possessive forms. “Our room” describes shared use here, not a transfer of legal ownership. Elena has never claimed to own the courtyard.

Compartir is a regular -ir verb, using chapter 4’s singular pattern: comparto, “I share”; compartes, “you share”; comparte, “he/she shares” or respectful “you share”. Comparto la llave means “I share the key”; ¿Compartes tu libro azul? means “Do you share your blue book?”; Usted comparte su libro means “You share your book”. The key passes to another reader and returns to the room. Sharing access to a key does not mean taking away the owner’s other belongings. A turno is an allocated turn or slot: one person reads while another waits; a family can also have a scheduled patio slot. Permiso means permission; ¿Permiso? asks permission to enter in this scene. A cartel is a sign or poster. Familia is family; madre/padre, mother/father; hermana/hermano, sister/brother; amigos, friends. These meanings are grounded by the delivered first-use aids and the characters’ actions before this explanation.

The reference examples translate as follows: mi casa / mis amigos, “my house / my friends”; tu nombre / tus amigos, “your name / your friends”; su caja / sus libros, “his box / his books” in the named contexts; nuestro patio / nuestra sala / nuestros libros / nuestras sillas, “our courtyard / our room / our books / our chairs”. The water has not been repaired away and the table has not been rebuilt. Location and ownership remain separate: a book can be in the shared room and still belong to a particular person.
